extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Baconian criteria for conducting and evaluating scientific inquiry (use of induction, handling definitions, avoiding intellectual idols). Focus is on how to form reliable definitions, gather and generalize from observations, and detect theoretical error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions must follow induction / be provisional
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions in the natural and material sciences should not be treated as final data; they ought to be framed only after the inductive stage of enquiry, and if ventured earlier they must be regarded as incomplete and provisional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reason deductively from premature definitions. 'It is only after we have completed the inductive stage of the enquiry that we are in a position to draw up a list of definitions, or, if we venture to do so before, we ought to regard them simply as incomplete and provisional.' Continually review and correct definitions as further instances and inductions are obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constant recurrence to particular instances (empirical grounding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific reasoning must repeatedly return to particular instances and series of instances to establish inductions and the properties on which definitions rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routinely collect and examine concrete examples; 'it is necessary... to be constantly recurring to particular instances.' Avoid leaping to general axioms without firm empirical support; build definitions and axioms from a solid base of observed cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify and rectify terminology continuously
rubrics_metrics.description: Words and common terminology are often inadequate or ambiguous and require continuous rectification and precise definition to express scientific concepts correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that words like 'idea, sense, cause, reason, substance' can change meaning and may not capture intended conceptions. Invest effort in precise technical terms and be prepared that others may not accept the newly attached sense; revise terms as understanding grows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware terms that name non-existent or ill-defined entities (Idola Fori)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some errors arise from names that refer to nothing or from names that inadequately or erroneously represent actual things or properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject or suspend judgment about verbally constructed entities with no empirical counterpart. Watch for names invented without verification (e.g., 'nameless' qualities later named as science advances) and avoid treating such names as evidence of real entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague qualitative descriptors without verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualities (except immediately sensed objects) are especially prone to vague, confused, or shifting definitions (e.g., 'humid', 'heavy', 'light', 'dense').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of broad qualitative labels that aggregate many distinct actions or properties. Use precise measurement or carefully distinguished subcategories instead of loose adjectives; the 'humid' example shows how a single term can be improperly abstracted from varied phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish mathematical from natural-science definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions in mathematics can often be constructed early and serve as stable abstractions; by contrast, definitions in natural sciences should follow careful induction and classification of properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat natural-science definitions as if they have the same epistemic status as mathematical definitions. In mathematics 'a single technical term is easily invented' and is rarely disputed; in nature, definitions must be grounded in observed, classified properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject untested inherited theories and perverse demonstrations (Idola Theatri)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretical systems and perverse laws of demonstration imported from authority can mislead inquiry; believers in such systems may so disagree on principles that argumentation is futile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept doctrines simply because they are traditional or elegant. Where principles are disputed, the entire argumentative edifice may be undermined. Use empirical tests to challenge and, if necessary, abandon received theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design methods and tools to reduce dependence on exceptional genius
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of discovery should not rely excessively on the acuteness of individual minds but should provide procedures and instruments that make correct results attainable by ordinary investigators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to using a rule or compass to draw a straight line or circle, develop standardized techniques that enable consistent results across practitioners. Strive for methods that 'nearly equalize' ordinary intellects rather than demand extraordinary genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid both over-generalizing from few experiments (empiricist error) and under-generalizing/vague axioms (rationalist/sophistic error)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two opposite methodological errors are (a) inferring too much from a small number of experiments, yielding 'monstrous' doctrines, and (b) forming too few or too vague fundamental inferences despite many facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical school risk: 'multum ex paucis' — too many inferences on too small a basis. Rational/sophistic school risk: 'parum ex multis' — too little secure inference from many facts. Balance breadth and depth of evidence: gather sufficient, varied experience before generalizing; ensure 'axiomata infima' are numerous and well-founded to support higher inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of philosophies mixing theology, tradition, or superstition (superstitious error)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some systems blend theology, authority, or belief in spirits/genii into explanations, which diverts inquiry from empirical causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against deriving scientific conclusions from faith, veneration, or tradition. Where investigation has been deflected by superstition, treat resulting doctrines as suspect and subject them to empirical scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch rhetorical elegance and narrative for misleading plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Fictitious narratives or elegant stories (as in the theatre) can make explanations seem more convincing or attractive without making them truer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake stylistic elegance or convincing narrative for evidential support. 'Narrationes fictae' can appear more 'concinnior' and 'elegantiores' yet be untrue; prioritize factual history and verified observation over rhetorical charm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expel false doctrines by continual rejection and antiquation
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain idols (false doctrines) can be expelled through steady negation and by antiquating the faulty theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a program of critical testing and abandonment of theories that fail empirical checks. Institutionalize practices that regularly displace vanae et falsae theoriae (vain and false theories) rather than preserving them by authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor external signs of theoretical weakness and causes of long-standing consensus in error
rubrics_metrics.description: The text warns that there are external signs by which one may detect that theories are poorly founded and notes there are causes for prolonged, general consensus in error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to signs such as overreliance on authority, lack of empirical variety, rhetorical insulation, or premature generality. Investigate sociological and methodological reasons why an error persists and design remedies (broader observation, new experiments, critical debate).
